r0_blindB_1.principle: Half of the attention heads compute their key at source position s from the previous position's state h[s-1], while the value comes from h[s] (no RoPE on these heads). A single layer therefore acts as a ready-made induction/copy head: "find where the current local context appeared before and copy the character that came next." That handles the many repeated identifiers and names in code from step 0, instead of hoping two-layer induction circuits form within only 3000 steps.

r0_blindB_2.principle: Give the network exact parser-state counters by summing learned per-character increments: 8 never-decaying cumulative sums plus 8 counters with a learned per-character reset, all fed to the model as tanh and cos(pi*c) features. These can learn bracket depth, quote parity (inside a string or not), column and line indentation directly, instead of a tiny transformer having to learn to count from attention in 3000 steps.

r0_blindA_1.principle: A cache head trained end to end, with the pointer mixed into the output. Each earlier position j keeps its final hidden state as a key and the character that actually followed it, x[j+1], as the value. The model mixes a sharp cosine-similarity copy distribution over those next characters into its softmax. Code reuses identifiers, keywords and whole phrases over and over, and this head gives exact long-range copying from step one. A tiny 2-layer transformer would otherwise have to discover induction-head composition inside 3000 steps.

r0_blindA_2.principle: Give the model an exact causal syntax register that costs no learning, computed with vectorised prefix scans of the input. It holds the column, the current line's indent, the previous non-blank line's indent and last character (for example ':'), the indent difference while inside leading whitespace, and the relative bracket depth, and it is embedded and added to the input. Leading whitespace and line structure make up a large share of Python characters and are fully fixed by these counts. Counting and comparing counts is exactly what a tiny attention model learns worst in 3000 steps. (This assumes the vocabulary is '\n' followed by chr(32..126) in order, so '\n'=0 and ' '=1.)

r1_count_1.principle: A copy head scores each earlier position j by the exact length of the shared character suffix ending at t and at j, computed with vectorised diagonal scans and capped at 12, plus a small learned content term. It then mixes the copy distribution over x[j+1] with the LM softmax through a learned null slot. Repeated identifiers, keywords and phrases in code are predicted by copying from the longest previous occurrence of the current context, like PPM. This works from step 0 instead of relying on a fuzzy match on a learned hidden state.

r1_count_2.principle: Treat source code as a 2D text grid. Every attention head gets a learned bias indexed by the exact (line distance 0..3, column difference within +-12) between query and key, computed with causal prefix scans. Indentation, dedents and aligned repeated statements are mostly decided by the character directly above, one line up, so one learned bias entry lets a head look straight up. Plain 1D positions cannot express this, because line lengths vary. It sits on the parent's shifted-key induction heads, with half the heads keyed on h[s-1].

r1_cross_1.principle: Both parents gain by putting exact input coordinates where a tiny transformer would otherwise have to learn them, so every head here keys source position s by the state just before it (h[s-1], value h[s]) and rotates by column (characters since the last newline, from a cummax scan) rather than by absolute position: one layer can then copy "what followed this context before" for repeated identifiers, and also "what followed at this same column on earlier lines", which gives indentation and vertical alignment with no syntax register at all.

r1_cross_2.principle: What both parents share is an exact, learning-free match on the preceding input, so this design computes it directly with no parameters: for every position, counts of which character followed each earlier occurrence of the last k characters (k = 1..8, from vectorised equality matrices), added to the logits as log(1+count) with a gate learned from the context; long matches copy repeated identifiers and phrases exactly from step 0, and matches that span newline-plus-spaces copy indentation and line structure, all on top of a plain small RoPE transformer.
